nodes.name: Every $w\in Y^{-\omega}$ lies in at least $k$ sets $T_g$
nodes.statement: Take $w\in Y^{-\omega}$ and let us prove that there exist at least $k$ elements $g\in G$ such that $w\in T_g$. The tiles $\tile\cdot g$ cover the limit $G$-space $\limGs[(G,X^*)]$, and we can find $g\in G$ such that if $x=\alpha^{-1}(y)$ for $y=\pi_{Y}(w\cdot g)\in\limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ then $x$ belongs to the tile $\tile$. Then $x$ is represented by the sequence $u\cdot 1$ for $u\in\xmo$. Equation~(\ref{eqn_theor_meraXY_mu tile }) implies $|V(u)|\geq k$ and so there exist $k$ elements $h_1,\ldots, h_k\in\nucl$ and sequences $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in\xmo$ such that for every $i$ there exists a left-infinite path in the nucleus $\nucl$ which ends in $h_i$ and is labeled by $(u,u_i)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} \[ x=\pi_X(u\cdot 1)=\pi_X(u_i\cdot h_i)\quad\mbox{ and }\quad x\cdot h_i^{-1}\in\tile \] for every $i=1,\ldots, k$. Then \[ \pi_Y(w\cdot gh_i^{-1})=\pi_Y(w\cdot g)h_i^{-1}=y\cdot h_i^{-1}=\alpha(x\cdot h_i^{-1})\in\alpha(\tile) \] and thus $w\in T_{gh_i^{-1}}$ for all $i=1,\ldots, k$.
nodes.statement_short: Transport the $k$ nucleus elements witnessing $|V(u)|\geq k$ through $\alpha$ to obtain $k$ indices $g$ with $w\in T_g$.

nodes.name: Integrate to get $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\tile))\geq k$
nodes.statement: Let $\chi_{T_g}$ be the characteristic function of the set $T_g$. Then $\sum_{g\in G}\chi_{T_g}(x)\geq k$ for almost all $x$. Integrating we get $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\tile))=\sum_{g\in G} \mu_u(T_g)\geq k=\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\tile)$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the multiplicity bound to get the first inequality.

nodes.name: Scaling inequality on tiles $\tile_v$
nodes.statement: Let us now show that $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\tile_v))\leq\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\tile_v)$ for any $v\in X^*$. Indeed, let $n=|v|$, then it follows from Theorem \ref{theor_limsX hom limsY} that $\alpha(\tile_v)=\alpha(\tau_v(\tile))=\tau_u(\alpha(\tile))g$ for some word $u\in Y^n$ and $g\in G$. Thus \begin{eqnarray*} \mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\tile_v))&=&\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\tau_u(\alpha(\tile)))\leq\frac{1}{|X|^n}\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\tile))=\\ &=&\frac{1}{|X|^n}\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\tile)=\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\tile_v). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Use $\alpha\tau_v=\tau_u\alpha$ up to translation and the $|X|^{-n}$ scaling to compare tile measures.

nodes.name: Absolute continuity of $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha$
nodes.statement: Let us prove that $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu_{(G,X^*)}$. Indeed, let $\mu_{(G,X^*)}(A)<\varepsilon$, $\pi^{-1}_{X}(A)=\cup_g T_g\cdot g$. Then $\sum_g\mu_u(T_g)<\varepsilon$. It follows that there exist $v_{i,g}\in X^*$ such that $T_g\subset\cup_i\xmo v_{i,g}$ and $\sum_{i,g}|X|^{-|v_{i,g}|}<\varepsilon$. Then $A\subset\cup_{i,g}\tile_{v_{i,g}}\cdot g$, and we have that $\sum_{i,g}\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\tile_{v_{i,g}})<\varepsilon\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\tile)$. Then $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(A))\leq\sum\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\tile_{v_{i,g}}))\leq\sum\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\tile_{v_{i,g}})<\varepsilon\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\tile)$. Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Cover small sets by cylinders/tiles of small total measure to get absolute continuity.

nodes.name: Reduce the inequality $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha\leq\mu_{(G,X^*)}$ to closed subsets of $\tile$
nodes.statement: We will now prove that $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha\leq\mu_{(G,X^*)}$. Since both $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha$ and $\mu_{(G,X^*)}$ are invariant under multiplication by $g\in G$ it suffices to prove this inequality for sets $A\subset\tile$. Since any Borel $A$ is a union of a closed set and a set of arbitrarily small measure, it suffices to prove the inequality for closed sets, as $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu_{(G,X^*)}$ by above.
nodes.statement_short: Use $G$-invariance and regularity to reduce to closed $A\subset\tile$.

nodes.name: Approximate a closed $A$ by unions of level-$n$ tiles
nodes.statement: So let $A\subset\tile$ be a closed set. For each $n$, let $A_n$ be the union of all tiles $\tile_v,v\in X^n,$ that have non-empty intersection with $A$. Let us show that $A=\cap_n A_n$. Suppose $x\in\cap A_n$, and $x$ is not in $A$. Then for each $n$ there is $v_n\in X^n$ such that $\tile_{v_n}$ has nonempty intersection with $A$ and $x\in\tile_{v_n}$. It follows that $x$ has some representation $u_nv_n\in\xmo$. Since the number of such representations is finite, we may choose subsequence $n_k$ such that $v_{n_k}$ is the beginning of some word $v\in\xmo$. Since $A$ is compact it follows that $A$ has nonempty intersection with $\cap_k\tile_{v_{n_k}}$, thus $\cap_k\tile_{v_{n_k}}$ contains at least two points, which is impossible. Since $A_n$ is the union of some tiles of level $n$, which are disjoint up to sets of measure $0$, the inequality also holds for all $A_n$. Going to the limit, we get the inequality for $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $A=\cap_n A_n$ by compactness, verify the inequality on each $A_n$ and pass to the limit.

nodes.name: Symmetry in $X$ and $Y$ gives equality
nodes.statement: By interchanging $X$ and $Y$ we get the reverse inequality, and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Swap the roles of $X$ and $Y$ to obtain the reverse inequality.

nodes.name: Proof that $\mathcal{U}$ is open, dense, of full measure and saturated
nodes.statement:
Construct the graph $\gr$ with the elements of $
ucl$ as vertices, for each edge labeled by $(x,x)$ in $
ucl$ we have the edge in $\gr$ with the same starting and end vertices, and labeled by $x$; and for each edge in $
ucl$ labeled by $(x,y)$ for $x
eq y$ there is an edge in $\gr$ with the same starting vertex that ends in the trivial element and labeled by $x$. Then the set $\mathcal{U}$ coincides with the set $\mathcal{O}(\gr)$. Indeed, $h\in V_{\gr}(w)$ if and only if there is a path in $
ucl$ labeled by $(w,w)$ that ends in $h$, thus $w\in\mathcal{U}$ if and only if $V_{\gr}(w)=\{1\}$. For every nontrivial element $h\in
ucl$ there exists a word $v\in X^{*}$ such that $h(v)
eq v$. It follows that there exists a path in the graph $\gr$ from $h$ to $1$. Hence the component $\{1\}$ is the only strongly connected component of the graph $\gr$ without outgoing edges. By Corollary~ef{cor_meas_sum_meas} the measure number of $\gr$ is $1$, and $\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{O}(\gr)$. The first statement of the lemma now follows from Lemma~ef{lemma_set V open dense}. Let us show that the set $\mathcal{U}$ is closed under the asymptotic equivalence relation (then the set $\mathcal{U}	imes G$ is also closed). It is sufficient to show that if there is a path in $
ucl$ labeled by $(u,v)$ and $u\in\mathcal{U}$ ($v\in\mathcal{U}$) then $v\in\mathcal{U}$ ($u\in\mathcal{U}$). Let the path in $
ucl$ labeled by $(u,v)$ end in $h$. It follows that $u$ is asymptotically equivalent to $v\cdot h$. Suppose there is a path in $
ucl$ labeled by $(v,v)$ that ends in $g$. It follows that $v$ is asymptotically equivalent to $v\cdot g$. Thus $u$ is asymptotically equivalent to $v\cdot gh$ which is asymptotically equivalent to $u\cdot h^{-1}gh$. By definition, there is a path in $
ucl$ labeled by $(u,u)$ which ends in $h^{-1}gh$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}$ we get $h^{-1}gh=1$, thus $g=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Realize $\mathcal{U}$ as $\mathcal{O}(\gr)$ for an auxiliary graph of measure number $1$, then transfer Lemma 1; saturation follows by conjugating the diagonal path.

nodes.name: Realize $\mathcal{U}$ as $\mathcal{O}(\gr)$ for an auxiliary graph
nodes.statement:
Construct the graph $\gr$ with the elements of $
ucl$ as vertices, for each edge labeled by $(x,x)$ in $
ucl$ we have the edge in $\gr$ with the same starting and end vertices, and labeled by $x$; and for each edge in $
ucl$ labeled by $(x,y)$ for $x
eq y$ there is an edge in $\gr$ with the same starting vertex that ends in the trivial element and labeled by $x$. Then the set $\mathcal{U}$ coincides with the set $\mathcal{O}(\gr)$. Indeed, $h\in V_{\gr}(w)$ if and only if there is a path in $
ucl$ labeled by $(w,w)$ that ends in $h$, thus $w\in\mathcal{U}$ if and only if $V_{\gr}(w)=\{1\}$. For every nontrivial element $h\in
ucl$ there exists a word $v\in X^{*}$ such that $h(v)
eq v$. It follows that there exists a path in the graph $\gr$ from $h$ to $1$. Hence the component $\{1\}$ is the only strongly connected component of the graph $\gr$ without outgoing edges. By Corollary~ef{cor_meas_sum_meas} the measure number of $\gr$ is $1$, and $\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{O}(\gr)$. The first statement of the lemma now follows from Lemma~ef{lemma_set V open dense}.
nodes.statement_short: Build $\gr$ from the nucleus so that $\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{O}(\gr)$ and $\mgr(\gr)=1$, then apply Lemma 1.

nodes.name: Saturation of $\mathcal{U}$ under asymptotic equivalence
nodes.statement:
Let us show that the set $\mathcal{U}$ is closed under the asymptotic equivalence relation (then the set $\mathcal{U}	imes G$ is also closed). It is sufficient to show that if there is a path in $
ucl$ labeled by $(u,v)$ and $u\in\mathcal{U}$ ($v\in\mathcal{U}$) then $v\in\mathcal{U}$ ($u\in\mathcal{U}$). Let the path in $
ucl$ labeled by $(u,v)$ end in $h$. It follows that $u$ is asymptotically equivalent to $v\cdot h$. Suppose there is a path in $
ucl$ labeled by $(v,v)$ that ends in $g$. It follows that $v$ is asymptotically equivalent to $v\cdot g$. Thus $u$ is asymptotically equivalent to $v\cdot gh$ which is asymptotically equivalent to $u\cdot h^{-1}gh$. By definition, there is a path in $
ucl$ labeled by $(u,u)$ which ends in $h^{-1}gh$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}$ we get $h^{-1}gh=1$, thus $g=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugate the diagonal loop at $v$ into one at $u$; triviality at $u$ forces $g=1$.

nodes.name: Proof that almost every point of $\lims$ has $|X|$ preimages
nodes.statement:
Since every point of $\lims$ has at most $|X|$ preimages under $\si$, it is enough to show that for almost every $w\in\xmo$ the map $\pi_{\lims[]}:\sigma^{-1}(w)ightarrow\si^{-1}(\pi_{\lims[]}(w))$ is one-to-one. Suppose that for some $w\in\xmo$ and $x
eq y$ in $X$ we have $\pi_{\lims[]}(wx)=\pi_{\lims[]}(wy)$. It follows that $wx,wy$ are asymptotically equivalent, thus there is a left-infinite path in $
ucl$ labeled by $(wx,wy)$. It follows that the prefix of this path labeled by $(w,w)$ must end in the nontrivial element, so $w
ot\in\mathcal{U}$. Since $\mu_u(\mathcal{U})=1$ by Lemma~ef{lemma U_open_dense_meas1}, we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to injectivity of $\pi$ on fibres; a collision forces $w\notin\mathcal{U}$, a null event.

nodes.name: Reduce to injectivity on the fibres of $\sigma$
nodes.statement: Since every point of $\lims$ has at most $|X|$ preimages under $\si$, it is enough to show that for almost every $w\in\xmo$ the map $\pi_{\lims[]}:\sigma^{-1}(w)\rightarrow\si^{-1}(\pi_{\lims[]}(w))$ is one-to-one.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the count to injectivity of $\pi_{\lims[]}$ on $\sigma^{-1}(w)$.

nodes.name: A collision forces $w\notin\mathcal{U}$
nodes.statement:
Suppose that for some $w\in\xmo$ and $x
eq y$ in $X$ we have $\pi_{\lims[]}(wx)=\pi_{\lims[]}(wy)$. It follows that $wx,wy$ are asymptotically equivalent, thus there is a left-infinite path in $
ucl$ labeled by $(wx,wy)$. It follows that the prefix of this path labeled by $(w,w)$ must end in the nontrivial element, so $w
ot\in\mathcal{U}$. Since $\mu_u(\mathcal{U})=1$ by Lemma~ef{lemma U_open_dense_meas1}, we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Identify collisions with a nontrivial diagonal path, i.e. $w\notin\mathcal{U}$, which is null.

nodes.name: Proof that $\rho|_{\tile_u}$ is a homeomorphism
nodes.statement: By definition, the map $\rho|_{\tile_u}:\tile_u\rightarrow\T_u$ is surjective, and $\tile_u$ is compact. Hence in order to prove that $\rho$ is a homeomorphism it is left to show that $\rho$ is injective on $\tile_u$. Take $x,y\in\tile_u$, and let $wu\in\xmo$ represent $x$ and $vu\in\xmo$ represent $y$. Suppose that $\rho(x)=\rho(y)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} it means that there is a left-infinite path in $\nucl$ labeled by $(wu,vu)$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$, this path must end in $1$. It follows, that $wu$ and $vu$ represent the same point of the tile $\tile_u$, and $x=y$. To prove the second claim, take $x\in\tile_u\cdot g\cap\tile_u\cdot g'$. Then $x$ is represented by two asymptotically equivalent sequences $wu\cdot g$ and $w'u\cdot g'$. It follows that there is a path in the nucleus $\nucl$ labeled by $(u,u)$ which ends in $g'g^{-1}$. Then $g=g'$ since $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Compactness plus injectivity (from $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ forcing diagonal paths to end in $1$) gives the homeomorphism, and the same argument gives disjointness of the $G$-translates.

nodes.name: Injectivity of $\rho$ on $\tile_u$
nodes.statement: By definition, the map $\rho|_{\tile_u}:\tile_u\rightarrow\T_u$ is surjective, and $\tile_u$ is compact. Hence in order to prove that $\rho$ is a homeomorphism it is left to show that $\rho$ is injective on $\tile_u$. Take $x,y\in\tile_u$, and let $wu\in\xmo$ represent $x$ and $vu\in\xmo$ represent $y$. Suppose that $\rho(x)=\rho(y)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} it means that there is a left-infinite path in $\nucl$ labeled by $(wu,vu)$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$, this path must end in $1$. It follows, that $wu$ and $vu$ represent the same point of the tile $\tile_u$, and $x=y$.
nodes.statement_short: $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ forces the connecting path to end in $1$, so $\rho$ is injective on $\tile_u$.

nodes.name: Disjointness of the translates $\tile_u\cdot g$
nodes.statement: To prove the second claim, take $x\in\tile_u\cdot g\cap\tile_u\cdot g'$. Then $x$ is represented by two asymptotically equivalent sequences $wu\cdot g$ and $w'u\cdot g'$. It follows that there is a path in the nucleus $\nucl$ labeled by $(u,u)$ which ends in $g'g^{-1}$. Then $g=g'$ since $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$.
nodes.statement_short: An overlap of translates yields a diagonal path ending in $g'g^{-1}$, forcing $g=g'$.

nodes.name: Proof that the projection is a covering map up to measure zero
nodes.statement: Consider the sets $\tilde{\limGs}=\pi_{\limGs[]}(\mathcal{U}\times G)$ and $\tilde{\lims}=\pi_{\lims[]}(\mathcal{U})$. It follows that $\tilde{\limGs}/G=\tilde{\lims}$. Since the set $\mathcal{U}$ has measure $1$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma U_open_dense_meas1}, the complements of $\mathcal{U}\times G$, of $\tilde{\limGs}$, and of $\tilde{\lims}$ have measure $0$. Since the group $G$ acts properly on $\limGs$, the same holds for $\tilde{\limGs}$. It is left to prove the freeness. Suppose $x\cdot g=x$ for $x\in\tilde{\limGs}$ and $g\in G$. Let $u\cdot h$ be a representative of $x$ in $\xmo\times G$. It follows that $u\cdot hg$ is asymptotically equivalent to $u\cdot h$, thus there is a path in $\nucl$ labeled by $(u,u)$ that ends in $h^{-1}gh$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}$ we have $g=1$. Hence the projection $\tilde{\limGs}\rightarrow\tilde{\lims}$ is a covering map, and the statement follows.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to the full-measure saturated sets coming from $\mathcal{U}$, where the $G$-action is proper and free, so the projection is a genuine covering.

nodes.name: Pass to the full-measure sets $\tilde{\limGs}$ and $\tilde{\lims}$
nodes.statement: Consider the sets $\tilde{\limGs}=\pi_{\limGs[]}(\mathcal{U}\times G)$ and $\tilde{\lims}=\pi_{\lims[]}(\mathcal{U})$. It follows that $\tilde{\limGs}/G=\tilde{\lims}$. Since the set $\mathcal{U}$ has measure $1$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma U_open_dense_meas1}, the complements of $\mathcal{U}\times G$, of $\tilde{\limGs}$, and of $\tilde{\lims}$ have measure $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the images of $\mathcal{U}$; their complements are null.

nodes.name: Freeness of the $G$-action on $\tilde{\limGs}$
nodes.statement: Since the group $G$ acts properly on $\limGs$, the same holds for $\tilde{\limGs}$. It is left to prove the freeness. Suppose $x\cdot g=x$ for $x\in\tilde{\limGs}$ and $g\in G$. Let $u\cdot h$ be a representative of $x$ in $\xmo\times G$. It follows that $u\cdot hg$ is asymptotically equivalent to $u\cdot h$, thus there is a path in $\nucl$ labeled by $(u,u)$ that ends in $h^{-1}gh$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}$ we have $g=1$.
nodes.statement_short: A fixed point would give a nontrivial diagonal path, impossible for $u\in\mathcal{U}$.

nodes.name: Conclude that the projection is a covering map
nodes.statement: Hence the projection $\tilde{\limGs}\rightarrow\tilde{\lims}$ is a covering map, and the statement follows.
nodes.statement_short: Free and proper action gives a covering map on the full-measure parts.

nodes.name: Proof that $\mu_{*}=\muls$
nodes.statement:
Consider the sets $	ilde{\lims}$ and $	ilde{\limGs}$ of full measure from the previous theorem. For every $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ we have $\T_u\subset	ilde{\lims}$, $	ile_u\cdot g\subset	ilde{\limGs}$ for every $g\in G$, and $ho^{-1}(\T_u)= igsqcup_{g\in G} 	ile_u\cdot g$ by Proposition~ef{x_j_homeo}. Since $	ilde{\lims}=\cup_{u\in\mathcal{U}^*}\T_u$ by Lemma~ef{lemma U_open_dense_meas1} it suffices to show that for any $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ the restriction of $\mu_{*}$ on $\T_u$ is equal to the restriction of $\muls$. Take a Borel set $A\subset	ile_u$ and consider its preimage $\pi^{-1}_{\limGs[]}(A)=\sqcup_{g\in
ucl} A_g\cdot g$. Then $\pi^{-1}_{\lims[]}(ho(A))=\sqcup_{g\in
ucl} A_g$. Here the union is disjoint because if $w\in{A_g\cap{}A_h}$ then $w\cdot g$ and $w\cdot h$ are asymptotically equivalent to $vu$ and $v'u$ respectively, for some $v,v'\in\xmo$. It follows that $vu\cdot g^{-1}$ is equivalent to $v'u\cdot h^{-1}$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}$, $g=h$. Hence \[ \muls(ho(A))=\mu_u(\pi^{-1}_{\lims[]}(ho(A)))=\mu_u(\sqcup_{g\in
ucl} A_g)=\sum_{g\in
ucl}\mu_u(A_g). \] By the property of the quotient measure \[ \mu_{*}(ho(A))=\mu(A)=\sum_{g\in
ucl}\mu_u(A_g)=\muls(ho(A)). \]
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to tiles $\T_u$ with $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$, where preimages split disjointly, so both measures compute the same sum $\sum_{g\in\nucl}\mu_u(A_g)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to the tiles $\T_u$ with $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$
nodes.statement: Consider the sets $\tilde{\lims}$ and $\tilde{\limGs}$ of full measure from the previous theorem. For every $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ we have $\T_u\subset\tilde{\lims}$, $\tile_u\cdot g\subset\tilde{\limGs}$ for every $g\in G$, and $\rho^{-1}(\T_u)=\bigsqcup_{g\in G} \tile_u\cdot g$ by Proposition~\ref{x_j_homeo}. Since $\tilde{\lims}=\cup_{u\in\mathcal{U}^*}\T_u$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma U_open_dense_meas1} it suffices to show that for any $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ the restriction of $\mu_{*}$ on $\T_u$ is equal to the restriction of $\muls$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to compare the two measures on the tiles $\T_u$, $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$.

nodes.name: Disjointness of the preimage decomposition
nodes.statement: Take a Borel set $A\subset\tile_u$ and consider its preimage $\pi^{-1}_{\limGs[]}(A)=\sqcup_{g\in\nucl} A_g\cdot g$. Then $\pi^{-1}_{\lims[]}(\rho(A))=\sqcup_{g\in\nucl} A_g$. Here the union is disjoint because if $w\in{A_g\cap{}A_h}$ then $w\cdot g$ and $w\cdot h$ are asymptotically equivalent to $vu$ and $v'u$ respectively, for some $v,v'\in\xmo$. It follows that $vu\cdot g^{-1}$ is equivalent to $v'u\cdot h^{-1}$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}$, $g=h$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $\pi^{-1}(\rho(A))$ into pieces $A_g$ and show the union is disjoint using $u\in\mathcal{U}$.

nodes.name: Both measures give $\sum_{g\in\nucl}\mu_u(A_g)$
nodes.statement:
Hence \[ \muls(ho(A))=\mu_u(\pi^{-1}_{\lims[]}(ho(A)))=\mu_u(\sqcup_{g\in
ucl} A_g)=\sum_{g\in
ucl}\mu_u(A_g). \] By the property of the quotient measure \[ \mu_{*}(ho(A))=\mu(A)=\sum_{g\in
ucl}\mu_u(A_g)=\muls(ho(A)). \]
nodes.statement_short: Compute both sides as $\sum_{g\in\nucl}\mu_u(A_g)$ and conclude equality.

nodes.name: Proof that $(\lims,\si,\muls)$ is Bernoulli
nodes.statement: We will use notions and results from \cite{hoffman:Bernoulli}. First recall that a measure preserving map with entropy $\log{d}$ is called {\it uniformly $d$-to-one endomorphism} if it is almost everywhere $d$-to-one and the conditional expectation of each preimage is $1/d$. The standard example is $(\xmo,\sigma,\mu_u)$, which is uniformly $|X|$-to-one. Next we want to show that $(\lims,\si,\muls)$ is also uniformly $|X|$-to-one. By Proposition~\ref{prop_measure_prop_lims} the map $\pi:\xmo\rightarrow\lims$ is injective on the preimages $\sigma^{-1}(w)$ for almost all $w\in\xmo$, that is, $\pi$ is {\it tree adapted} in terminology of \cite{hoffman:Bernoulli}. We can apply Lemma~2.3 from \cite{hoffman:Bernoulli}, which says that a tree adapted factor of a uniform $d$-to-one endomorphism is again uniform $d$-to-one endomorphism. In particular, the shift $\si$ is the map of maximal entropy $\log |X|$. To prove the theorem, we use the following Theorem~5.5 in \cite{hoffman:Bernoulli}. \begin{theor} A uniform $d$-to-one endomorphism $(Y,S,\mu)$ is one-sidedly conjugated to the one-sided Bernoulli $d$-shift if and only if there exists a generating function $f$ so that $(Y,S,\mu)$ and $f$ are tree very weak Bernoulli. \end{theor} Recall the definition of tree very weak Bernoulli and generating function. Let $(Y,S,\mu)$ be uniformly $d$-to-one and $f:Y\rightarrow{R}$ be a tree adapted function to a compact metric space $R$ with metric $D$. The function $f$ is called \textit{generating} if the $\sigma$-algebra on $Y$ is generated by $S^{-i}f^{-1}(\mathcal{B}),i\geq{0}$, where $\mathcal{B}$ is the $\sigma$-algebra of Borel sets of the space $R$. Informally, ``tree very weak Bernoulli'' means that for almost all pairs of points in $Y$ their trees of preimages are close. To give a formal definition note that since $S$ is uniformly $d$-to-one, for almost all points $y\in Y$ the set $S^{-k}(y)$ contains exactly $d^k$ points, i.e. the tree of preimages is a $d$-regular rooted tree. The set $\{1,\ldots, d\}^{*}$ of finite words over $\{1,\ldots,d\}$ can be considered as a $d$-regular rooted tree, where every word $v$ is connected with $vx$ for $x\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$, and the root is the empty word $\emptyset$. We can use the tree $\{1,\ldots, d\}^{*}$ to label the trees of preimages. For almost all points $y\in Y$ there is a map $T_y:\{1,\dots,d\}^*\rightarrow{Y}$ such that $T_y(\emptyset)=y$ and $T_y(\sigma(v))=S(T_y(v))$ for all nonempty words $v\in \{1,\dots,d\}^*$. Every map $T_y$ is tree adapted, and it is uniquely defined up to an automorphism of the tree $\{1,\dots,d\}^*$. Then $(Y,S,\mu)$ and $f$ are called {\it tree very weak Bernoulli} if for any $\varepsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$ there is a set $W=W(\varepsilon,n)\subset Y$ with $\mu(W)>1-\varepsilon$ such that for any $y,y'\in{W}$ \begin{equation} t_n(y,y')=\min_\psi \frac{1}{n}\sum_{v\in \{1,\dots,d\}^{*}, |v|\leq n}d^{-|v|}D(f(T_y(v)),f(T_{y'}(\psi(v))))<\varepsilon, \end{equation} where the minimum is taken over all automorphisms $\psi$ of the tree $\{1,\dots,d\}^*$. Notice that the definition of $t_n$ does not depend on the choice of $T_y$. Let us show that $(\lims,\si,\muls)$ is tree very weak Bernoulli for the identity map $id:\lims\rightarrow\lims$. It immediately follows that $id$ is tree adapted and generating. Take a point $x\in\lims$ and let $x$ be represented by some $w\in\xmo$. Define the map $T_x:X^{*}\rightarrow\lims$ by the rule $T_x(v)=\pi(wv)$. It is enough to show that $ t_n(x,x')\rightarrow 0, n\rightarrow\infty, $ for almost all $x,x'\in\lims$. Using (\ref{eqn_diam_tile_goes_zero}) we can find $n_1$ such that $\max_{v\in X^n}\rm{diam}(\T_v)<\epsilon/2$ for all $n\geq n_1$. It means that $D(\pi(wv),\pi(w'v))<\epsilon/2$ for all $v,|v|\geq n_1$ (here $D$ is a fixed metric on the limit space $\lims$). Thus, taking $\psi$ to be the identical tree automorphism, we have that \[ t_n(x,x')<\frac{n_1}{n} \rm{diam}(\lims)+\frac{n-n_1}{n}\frac{\epsilon}{2}<\frac{n_1}{n} \rm{diam}(\lims)+\frac{\epsilon}{2}<\epsilon \] for $n>2n_1\rm{diam}(\lims)/\epsilon$. Hence $(\lims,\si,\muls)$ and $id$ are tree very weak Bernoulli, which finishes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\si$ is uniformly $|X|$-to-one via tree-adaptedness of $\pi$, then verify the tree-very-weak-Bernoulli condition for $f=id$ using that tile diameters shrink, and apply the Hoffman-Rudolph criterion.

nodes.name: $(\lims,\si,\muls)$ is uniformly $|X|$-to-one
nodes.statement: We will use notions and results from \cite{hoffman:Bernoulli}. First recall that a measure preserving map with entropy $\log{d}$ is called {\it uniformly $d$-to-one endomorphism} if it is almost everywhere $d$-to-one and the conditional expectation of each preimage is $1/d$. The standard example is $(\xmo,\sigma,\mu_u)$, which is uniformly $|X|$-to-one. Next we want to show that $(\lims,\si,\muls)$ is also uniformly $|X|$-to-one. By Proposition~\ref{prop_measure_prop_lims} the map $\pi:\xmo\rightarrow\lims$ is injective on the preimages $\sigma^{-1}(w)$ for almost all $w\in\xmo$, that is, $\pi$ is {\it tree adapted} in terminology of \cite{hoffman:Bernoulli}. We can apply Lemma~2.3 from \cite{hoffman:Bernoulli}, which says that a tree adapted factor of a uniform $d$-to-one endomorphism is again uniform $d$-to-one endomorphism. In particular, the shift $\si$ is the map of maximal entropy $\log |X|$.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi$ is tree adapted, so by Hoffman-Rudolph Lemma 2.3 the factor $(\lims,\si,\muls)$ is uniformly $|X|$-to-one of maximal entropy.

nodes.name: Invoke the Hoffman-Rudolph criterion
nodes.statement: To prove the theorem, we use the following Theorem~5.5 in \cite{hoffman:Bernoulli}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the theorem to verifying the tree-very-weak-Bernoulli property.

nodes.name: Verify tree very weak Bernoulli for $f=id$
nodes.statement: Let us show that $(\lims,\si,\muls)$ is tree very weak Bernoulli for the identity map $id:\lims\rightarrow\lims$. It immediately follows that $id$ is tree adapted and generating. Take a point $x\in\lims$ and let $x$ be represented by some $w\in\xmo$. Define the map $T_x:X^{*}\rightarrow\lims$ by the rule $T_x(v)=\pi(wv)$. It is enough to show that $ t_n(x,x')\rightarrow 0, n\rightarrow\infty, $ for almost all $x,x'\in\lims$. Using (\ref{eqn_diam_tile_goes_zero}) we can find $n_1$ such that $\max_{v\in X^n}\rm{diam}(\T_v)<\epsilon/2$ for all $n\geq n_1$. It means that $D(\pi(wv),\pi(w'v))<\epsilon/2$ for all $v,|v|\geq n_1$ (here $D$ is a fixed metric on the limit space $\lims$). Thus, taking $\psi$ to be the identical tree automorphism, we have that \[ t_n(x,x')<\frac{n_1}{n} \rm{diam}(\lims)+\frac{n-n_1}{n}\frac{\epsilon}{2}<\frac{n_1}{n} \rm{diam}(\lims)+\frac{\epsilon}{2}<\epsilon \] for $n>2n_1\rm{diam}(\lims)/\epsilon$. Hence $(\lims,\si,\muls)$ and $id$ are tree very weak Bernoulli, which finishes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Shrinking tile diameters bound $t_n(x,x')$ by $\epsilon$ using the identity tree automorphism.

nodes.name: Proof that $\Phi_*\mu$ is the right Haar measure
nodes.statement: The measure $\Phi_*\mu$ is a non-zero regular Borel measure on $L$. It is left to prove that it is translation invariant. Since the measure $\mu$ is $G$-invariant and the map $\Phi$ is $G$-equivariant, the measure $\Phi_*\mu$ is $G$-invariant. By the property of the map $\Phi$ we have $\phi_L(\Phi(A))=\Phi(\tau_{x_0}(A))g_0$ for every Borel set $A\subset\limGs$. Notice that since the map $\phi$ is injective, we get $\mu(A)=|X|\mu(\tau_x(A))$ (see the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop_measure lims propert}) and hence $\Phi_*\mu(B)=|X|\Phi_*\mu(\phi_L(B))$ for every Borel set $B\subset L$. It follows that the measure $\Phi_*\mu$ is $\cup_n \phi_L^n(G)$-invariant. Since $\phi_L$ is contracting, the set $\cup_n \phi_L^n(G)$ is dense in the Lie group $L$. Hence $\Phi_*\mu$ is $L$-invariant.
nodes.statement_short: $G$-invariance plus the scaling relation under $\phi_L$ gives invariance under the dense subgroup $\cup_n\phi_L^n(G)$, hence under all of $L$.

nodes.name: $\Phi_*\mu$ is a non-zero $G$-invariant regular Borel measure
nodes.statement: The measure $\Phi_*\mu$ is a non-zero regular Borel measure on $L$. It is left to prove that it is translation invariant. Since the measure $\mu$ is $G$-invariant and the map $\Phi$ is $G$-equivariant, the measure $\Phi_*\mu$ is $G$-invariant.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to translation invariance and get $G$-invariance from equivariance of $\Phi$.

nodes.name: Upgrade to $L$-invariance by density of $\cup_n\phi_L^n(G)$
nodes.statement: By the property of the map $\Phi$ we have $\phi_L(\Phi(A))=\Phi(\tau_{x_0}(A))g_0$ for every Borel set $A\subset\limGs$. Notice that since the map $\phi$ is injective, we get $\mu(A)=|X|\mu(\tau_x(A))$ (see the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop_measure lims propert}) and hence $\Phi_*\mu(B)=|X|\Phi_*\mu(\phi_L(B))$ for every Borel set $B\subset L$. It follows that the measure $\Phi_*\mu$ is $\cup_n \phi_L^n(G)$-invariant. Since $\phi_L$ is contracting, the set $\cup_n \phi_L^n(G)$ is dense in the Lie group $L$. Hence $\Phi_*\mu$ is $L$-invariant.
nodes.statement_short: The scaling identity under $\phi_L$ gives invariance under a dense subgroup, hence under $L$.

nodes.name: Proof that $\Phi_*\mu$ is the Lebesgue measure
nodes.statement: The measure $\Phi_*\mu$ is the Haar measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ by the above example. Since the Haar measure is unique up to multiplicative constant, we have that $\Phi_*\mu=c\lambda$ for some constant $c>0$ and we need to prove that $c=1$. Recall that $\mu(\tile)$ is integer by Proposition~\ref{theor_tile_measure}, and almost every point of $\limGs$ is covered by $\mu(\tile)$ tiles $\tile\cdot g$ by Proposition~\ref{points_above}. Hence $\Phi_*\mu(T)=\Phi_*\mu(\Phi(\tile))=\mu(\tile)$ is integer and almost every point of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by $\mu(\tile)$ tiles $T+g$, $g\in\Z^n$, with respect to the measure $\Phi_*\mu$, and thus with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\lambda$. It follows that, if $\chi_{T+g}$ is the characteristic function of $T+g$, then $\sum_{g\in\Z^n}\chi_{T+g}=\mu(\tile)$ almost everywhere with respect to both measures. Hence \[ \Phi_*\mu(T)=\mu(\tile)=\int_I\sum_{g\in\Z^n}\chi_{T+g}d\lambda=\sum_{g\in\Z^n}\int_{I+g}\chi_T d\lambda=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\chi_T d\lambda=\lambda(T), \] where $I$ is the unit cube in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Since $\mu(\tile)$ is positive, $c=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of Haar measure gives $\Phi_*\mu=c\lambda$; computing both sides on $T$ via the constant multiplicity $\sum_g\chi_{T+g}=\mu(\tile)$ pins $c=1$.

nodes.name: Reduce to determining the constant $c$
nodes.statement: The measure $\Phi_*\mu$ is the Haar measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ by the above example. Since the Haar measure is unique up to multiplicative constant, we have that $\Phi_*\mu=c\lambda$ for some constant $c>0$ and we need to prove that $c=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of Haar measure reduces the claim to showing $c=1$.

nodes.name: Constant covering multiplicity of the translates $T+g$

nodes.statement_short: Transport the perfect multiple covering to $\mathbb{R}^n$: $\sum_g\chi_{T+g}=\mu(\tile)$ a.e.

nodes.name: Integrate over the unit cube to get $c=1$
nodes.statement: Hence \[ \Phi_*\mu(T)=\mu(\tile)=\int_I\sum_{g\in\Z^n}\chi_{T+g}d\lambda=\sum_{g\in\Z^n}\int_{I+g}\chi_T d\lambda=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\chi_T d\lambda=\lambda(T), \] where $I$ is the unit cube in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Since $\mu(\tile)$ is positive, $c=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrating the multiplicity over the unit cube gives $\Phi_*\mu(T)=\lambda(T)$, so $c=1$.

nodes.name: Set up the eigenvalue-$1$ system and its free entries
nodes.statement: a left eigenvector of $T_p$ for the eigenvalue $1$ is uniquely defined if we know its entries $\mu_p(B_v)$ for vertices $v$ in the strongly connected components of $\gr$ without outgoing edges.
nodes.statement_short: The eigenvector is determined once the entries on the sink strongly connected components are known.

nodes.name: Initialize the entries on the sink components
nodes.statement: For every such a component $\gr'$, we have $B_v=\xo$ and $\mu_p(B_v)=1$ for every vertex $v\in\gr'$ if the component $\gr'$ is a strictly right-resolving graph, and $\mu_p(B_v)=0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Set $\mu_p(B_v)=1$ on strictly right-resolving sink components and $0$ otherwise.

nodes.name: Build the label product graph on $V\times V$
nodes.statement: Construct a new graph $\mathscr{G}$ with the set of vertices $V\times V$ and put an edge from $(v,u)$ to $(v',u')$ labeled by $x\in X$ for every edges $v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow v'$ and $u\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u'$ in the graph $\gr$ (label products of graphs by Definition~3.4.8 in \cite{IntroSymbDyn}).
nodes.statement_short: Form the label product of $\gr$ with itself.

nodes.name: Read off the intersection as a single $B$-set
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that then $B_{(v,u)}=B_v\cap B_u$ (see Proposition~3.4.10 in \cite{IntroSymbDyn}).
nodes.statement_short: Return $B_{(v,u)}=B_v\cap B_u$, reducing the problem to the single-graph case.
